report:
Based on this research, the answer is more nuanced than a flat "no" — the evidence has shifted over time.

**Report**

Older Cochrane reviews (through 2010) and meta-analyses reported that probiotics, given with rehydration therapy, shortened acute infectious diarrhea by roughly 24–25 hours and reduced stool frequency (cochranelibrary.com; racgp.org.au). However, these earlier trials were often small, heterogeneous, and used varied probiotic strains/doses, limiting confidence.

More recent, higher-quality evidence has weakened this conclusion substantially. The updated 2020 Cochrane review states that probiotics "may not affect how long acute diarrhoea lasts" and that clinicians "do not know if they can shorten the time to recovery" — downgrading certainty due to inconsistency and risk of bias (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea). This shift was driven partly by two large, rigorous, placebo-controlled U.S. multicenter trials in children with acute gastroenteritis (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG alone, and a combination probiotic), both published in NEJM in 2018, which found no significant benefit on diarrhea duration, severity, or need for follow-up care (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597).

At the same time, some newer meta-analyses pooling numerous smaller trials (2023–2025) still report modest benefits — e.g., diarrhea resolving about one day earlier — but rate the certainty of evidence as "very low," reflecting continued heterogeneity across probiotic strains and study quality (sciencedirect.com; frontiersin.org).

**Conclusion:** The claim that probiotics do *not* shorten acute infectious diarrhea is reasonably well-supported by the most rigorous, high-quality evidence (Cochrane 2020, large NEJM RCTs), even though many smaller/older studies suggested modest benefit. The overall picture is one of uncertain, likely minimal clinical benefit rather than definitive proof of no effect.
